Climb
klīm
v. (to ascend by effort, hand and foot; used of soldiers, of fugitives, and of a flight from God that does not succeed)
Old English climban, akin to cleave — to go up by clinging. The Hebrew alah is the ordinary verb of going up, the same word used of offering a burnt sacrifice, which goes up in smoke.

Biblical Definition

Men climb in Scripture for three reasons: to escape, to attack, and to hide from God. To escape: “The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks” (Jer 4:29). To attack, in Joel's terrible picture of the locust army that is also an army of men: “They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks” (Joe 2:7), and again, “they shall climb up upon the houses; they shall enter in at the windows like a thief” (Joe 2:9). And to hide, which is the use that matters most: “Though they dig into hell, thence shall mine hand take them; though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down” (Amo 9:2). Amos piles the impossibilities up — the top of Carmel, the bottom of the sea — and every one of them ends in the same hand. David had already turned the same fact into comfort rather than terror: “If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there” (Psa 139:8). It is the same doctrine; only the man's standing before God differs.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to climb as to creep up by little and little, or with labor; to mount or ascend by means of the hands and feet; and figuratively, to rise to a higher condition with effort.

expand to see more

CLIMB, v.i. clime. To creep up by little and little, or step by step; to mount or ascend with labor and difficulty.

They shall climb the wall like men of war. Joel ii.

2. To rise or ascend with labor or difficulty; as, to climb to preferment.

CLIMB, v.t. To ascend by means of the hands and feet, implying labor.

Key Scripture

Joe 2:7 — "They shall run like mighty men; they shall climb the wall like men of war; and they shall march every one on his ways, and they shall not break their ranks:"

Amo 9:2 — "Though they dig into hell, thence shall mine hand take them; though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down:"

Psa 139:8 — "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there."

Jer 4:29 — "The whole city shall flee for the noise of the horsemen and bowmen; they shall go into thickets, and climb up upon the rocks: every city shall be forsaken, and not a man dwell therein."

Modern Corruption

The omnipresence of God is presented almost solely as a comfort, though Amos 9:2 states it first as the reason no man escapes judgment.

expand to see more

Psalm 139 is quoted constantly and Amos 9 almost never, yet they assert the same attribute in nearly the same words. God is in heaven and in hell, on Carmel's top and in the sea's bottom; there is no coordinate at which a creature is out of reach. To David this is the ground of a settled peace, because he has said in the same psalm, search me, O God, and know my heart. To the men of Amos's generation the identical truth is the announcement that flight is pointless. Omnipresence is not in itself a comfort; it is a comfort to the reconciled and a terror to the fugitive, and a doctrine of God trimmed to yield only reassurance has stopped being a doctrine of God. Jonah is the narrative proof, since he went down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sea and down into the fish, and every descent brought him nearer the God he was fleeing.

Joel's climbers give the other application. His army mounts the wall in ranks, every one on his own way, and they do not break their ranks or thrust one another — a discipline more frightening than fury. It is a picture of judgment arriving in good order, and the prophet's response to it is not a strategy but a summons: turn ye even to me with all your heart, and rend your heart, and not your garments. The modern habit is to read every threatening passage as a metaphor for internal difficulty and every promise as a literal guarantee. Joel does the reverse. The locusts and the army are real, the wall really falls, and the mercy offered in the middle of it is real too, for the LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew alah (H5927), to go up, ascend, climb — also the verb behind the burnt offering that goes up; with yarad (H3381), to go down, its constant counterpart.

expand to see more

Hebrew alah (H5927) — to go up, to ascend, to climb; they shall climb the wall like men of war; Joel 2:7.

Hebrew olah (H5930) — a burnt offering, literally that which goes up; from the same root as climb; Leviticus 1:3.

Hebrew yarad (H3381) — to go down; the LORD will bring down those who climb up to heaven; Amos 9:2.

Hebrew sheol (H7585) — the grave, the place of the dead; if I make my bed in hell, thou art there; Psalm 139:8.

Greek anabaino (G305) — to go up, to ascend; Zacchaeus climbed a sycomore tree to see Jesus; Luke 19:4.

Usage

"“They shall climb the wall like men of war” — judgment arriving in good order."

"“Though they climb up to heaven, thence will I bring them down” — the flight that has no destination."

"“If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there” — the same truth, and a different man saying it."
